results.summary: This design implements a Jeopardy-style gameshow buzzer that drives a 7-segment display. It takes a clock and reset input and outputs the seven segments plus a dot. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how the buzzer works or how to test it. As a result, the exact functionality and usage cannot be determined from the provided information.

ttFIR implements a 4-tap digital finite impulse response (FIR) filter with 6-bit two's complement inputs and coefficients and an 8-bit output. Coefficients are loaded serially over four clock cycles, and input samples are shifted in each cycle; the output is the 8 most significant bits of the 14-bit sum, delayed by two cycles. The design is intended to be driven by an FPGA or microcontroller that provides the input signal and reads the output. It is a straightforward DSP building block, and the author suggests increasing the number of taps as a future challenge.

The CRC Decelerator is a reconfigurable CRC engine that can be programmed to compute any CRC up to 32 bits with arbitrary length streamed input data. It uses a 2-bit command interface and a 4-bit data path to stream in configuration parameters, message nibbles, and to read out the final CRC value. The design is a follow-up to a full-custom VLSI CRC-32 datapath and is intended for low-speed operation, hence the name 'decelerator'. It requires no external hardware beyond a host that can drive the pins according to the documented protocol.

This design implements an 8-bit configurable Galois linear-feedback shift register (LFSR). It has three modes: normal shift, set shift register, and set XOR mask, allowing the user to configure the feedback polynomial. Data is loaded 4 bits at a time over two cycles, and the full 8-bit state is available on the outputs. The documentation is minimal, but the pin names and description indicate the basic operation.

This is a random number guessing game where the player has three attempts to guess a 6-bit random number. The guess is entered on six input pins, and the result appears on six output pins, with each bit indicating whether the corresponding guess bit matched the random number. A correct guess outputs all ones and resets the game with a new random number; after three failed attempts, the game outputs all zeros and resets. The design uses Verilog's $random function and is intended as a simple interactive game.

ezm_cpu is a basic 8-bit CPU implemented in Verilog. It provides a program counter output and six input pins, and it requires external hardware such as RAM and a decoder or an FPGA with a programmed ROM to function. The documentation is very sparse, giving only a brief description and no details on the instruction set or architecture. Testing requires connecting the external memory and decoder as described.

This design implements a digital temperature sensor that measures on-chip temperature and displays it on a 7-segment LED display. It creatively uses tristate inverters to build a voltage DAC and bias an NMOS transistor in subthreshold operation, exploiting the temperature dependence of subthreshold current to create a temperature-dependent delay. A calibration engine with a look-up table allows linearization and calibration of the displayed temperature code. The sensor outputs a 0-63 code, showing tens and ones on the display, and includes debug modes for internal signals.

MicroTapeout contains 395 standard cells from the sky130_fd_sc_hd library, with a multiplexing mechanism to expose any cell to the input/output pins. It allows low-level digital design engineers to test individual standard cells and gain timing insights. The design includes an experimental timing circuit that uses a ring oscillator and counter to measure cell switching times. Testing involves selecting pages and inputs via the pins, and the design is notable for its large number of cells and educational purpose.

QTChallenges implements eight different benchmark circuits, all generated by ChatGPT-4, selectable via three input pins. The benchmarks include a shift register, sequence generator, sequence detector, ABRO state machine, binary-to-BCD converter, LFSR, traffic light controller, and dice roller. While all designs passed their ChatGPT-created testbenches, several are functionally incorrect due to inadequate testbenches, such as the dice roller which has a constant output. The project serves as an experiment in AI-generated hardware design and includes full transcripts of the ChatGPT conversations.

The MSF Clock decodes the MSF radio clock bitstream and displays the time on an LED display driven by a shift register. It requires an external MSF receiver module connected to the data input, and a 12.5 kHz clock. The design outputs shift clock, data, and latch signals to drive a 42-bit shift register chain for the display, and can also show the date when a button is held. It is a specialized timekeeping design that synchronizes and decodes the MSF time signal.
